english_translation: Brand-new tools made of steel and wood are displayed on view, including brushes, rakes, and shovels.

dialogue.shona: Midziyo mitsva yakaiswa panoonekera. Yakagadzirwa nesimbi nedanda. Pane midziyo inosanganisira maburasho, poitawo mareki namafoshora.
dialogue.english: Brand-new tools made of metal and wood are on display, including brushes, rakes, and shovels.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Midziyo [midziyo] • mitsva [mitsva] • yakaiswa [it (past) iswa] • panoonekera [on / at noonekera] • Yakagadzirwa [it (past) gadzirwa] • nesimbi [and / with simbi] • nedanda [and / with danda] • Pane [on / at ne]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakaiswa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakaiswa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('inosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'inosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nesimbi'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nesimbi'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'simbi' forms 'nesimbi'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Hardware Stores & Garden Implements ('Maburasho, Mareki, Mafoshora')
cultural_notes.content: Because most Zimbabwean households maintain a yard, orchard, or kitchen garden, hardware stores stock sturdy steel-and-timber tools ('midziyo yakagadzirwa nesimbi nedanda') including rakes ('mareki'), shovels ('mafoshora'), and brushes.

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tora mvura uinwe.'
options: Take the water and drink it.
Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Come here and help me carry the books.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

active_exercises.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?
options: Bread and sugar because it is morning
Milk or water because they feel thirsty
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal
active_exercises.correct_answer: Milk or water because they feel thirsty
